questions.topic: A Class And The Object Made From It
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a class from an instance built from it
questions.stem: A program defines a class and then builds two objects from it. Which statement about the class and those two objects is correct?

The class is one of the objects, and the other two are copies of it

The answer calling the class an object is the belief to rule out first, because the class is what makes the objects rather than one of them.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Who Each Text Form Is Written For
questions.learningObjective: explain the separate audiences the two text forms of an object serve
questions.stem: A class defines a form aimed at a developer reading a failed report and a form aimed at a person reading a receipt. Explain what each form is for, and what happens if the class defines only the developer form.

answer.exemplar: The two forms exist because there are two different readers with two different questions. The form aimed at a developer is what a person or a tool sees when the object appears inside a container or inside a failure report, and its job is to say unambiguously what the object holds, so a value that could be rebuilt from the text is the right bar and the class name belongs in it. The form aimed at a person is what a user sees when the object is printed on its own or placed into a message, and its job is to read well, which is why a currency amount is a better fit there than a constructor-style rendering. Defining only the developer form is a real and common choice, and the language then uses it in both places, so the receipt inherits an implementation-looking string with brackets and a class name in it. That is not a crash, it is a small piece of carelessness that shows up in whatever the user is shown. The reason to define both is that the two are cheap, that each is short, and that a class whose only text form is the developer one tends to have its user-facing output changed by someone tidying up the developer form, which then quietly alters what users see. There is one detail worth knowing about the fallback in the other direction. If a class defines only the person form, the developer form is derived from it, and the result is an unambiguous class name and address rather than anything reconstructing, so the failure is visible and diagnosable. If a class defines both, the developer form is used inside containers and the person form is used outside them, and that split is the whole reason both exist. Where a class has no meaningful person-facing rendering, it is better to leave the developer form as the only one deliberately than to invent a decorative text for it.

questions.explanation: The developer form exists so a value inside a container or a failure report can be read back and reconstructed, and the person form exists so a value shown on its own reads well, and containers and direct conversions choose differently for that reason. The tempting simplification is to define one and let it serve both, which produces a receipt showing brackets and a class name, and the language's fallback in the other direction is worth knowing because a missing developer form yields a visible address rather than a silently wrong reconstruction.
questions.hint: Ask who reads each form, and which places each is used in.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why Equality And Hashing Must Agree
questions.learningObjective: explain the consistency two hooks owe each other
questions.stem: A class declares that two of its objects are equal when their names match without regard to case, and it hashes the names with the case left in. Explain what goes wrong inside a set or a table, and what the two hooks owe each other.

answer.exemplar: The two hooks owe each other a single rule: objects that compare equal must hash equally. The reason is that a set and a table use hashing as their first filter and only compare the two hooks when the hashes match, so if two equal objects hash differently the second one never reaches the comparison at all. In this class the comparison ignores case while the hash does not, so the two objects that the class insists are equal land in different places and both are kept. Every operation that relies on finding an existing member is then unreliable in a way that is not obvious from the outside. Adding a second equal object grows the set. Looking an object up fails to find one already in it. Removing one leaves its equal twin behind. Each of these is a symptom of the same single disagreement, and a program that only ever adds and never looks up can appear to work for a long time, which is what makes the bug survive into production. The fix is not to weaken the comparison but to make the hash derive from the same normalised value the comparison uses, so the two agree by construction rather than by coincidence. There is a second direction worth stating, because it constrains the design rather than the implementation. An object that says it is equal to nothing is unhashable, which is the language refusing to let a mutable value be used as a key at all, and that refusal is a feature: a value that can be hashed but changes afterwards would be unfindable the moment it changed. This is why a class that declares equality for a mutable value is usually declaring a mistake, and why the pairing of a comparison hook and a hashing hook only works for values that are fixed once built. The practical habit is to write the two hooks so that they read the same expression, and to add a test that puts an equal pair into a set and asserts the set has one member, because that test is the only one that fails when the two drift apart.

The rule the two hooks owe each other is that equal objects must hash equally, and the fix is to derive both from the same normalised value rather than to weaken the comparison. The other direction matters too, since a class that claims equality with everything cannot be used as a key at all, and that refusal is the language protecting a table from a value that could change after insertion.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Setup Scope Decides
questions.learningObjective: explain how a setup's scope turns one test's leftovers into another's input
questions.stem: Two tests pass when run one after another and one of them fails when it is run alone. Explain how a shared setup can produce that, and what a test that avoids the problem has to guarantee.

answer.exemplar: A setup that is created once and reused hands every test the same object, so anything one test writes is still there when the next test starts, and the second test is then a function of the first as well as of its own inputs. Run alone, the same test starts from a clean object and takes a different path, which is why the failure appears and disappears with the order. The mechanism is not subtle once it is named: state that outlives a test is state the test does not own, and the test's result stops being a statement about its subject and becomes a statement about the run. What a test has to guarantee is that everything it depends on is either created for it, or is something it treats as read-only, and that it leaves nothing behind for anyone else. Creating for it is the narrow setup, run once per test, and it is the right default for anything a test writes to. Treating something as read-only is the wide setup, run once for the whole run, and it is the right choice only for expensive work whose result no test may modify, such as loading a shared reference table, and the discipline has to be enforced rather than assumed, because one test that writes to it reintroduces the same bug with a longer fuse. There is a third option worth knowing, which is to have the wide setup hand out copies of its result, so the cost is paid once and each test still gets something it may write to. The diagnostic is worth remembering too. If a test fails only in a run and not alone, the run is supplying the input it did not write, and the first move is to print the shared object at the start of the failing test, which usually shows the previous test's leftovers immediately. Running the suite in a different order, or running each test alone, is a cheap way to make the dependence visible before any of the code is changed.

questions.explanation: A setup that runs once hands every test the same object, so a test that writes to it is fed by whatever the earlier test left, and run alone it starts clean and behaves differently. The guarantee a test needs is that what it depends on was created for it or is treated as read-only, and that it leaves nothing behind. The tempting fix is to widen the setup for speed, which is right for expensive read-only work and wrong for anything a test may write, and the cheap diagnostic is to run the tests alone and in a different order to make the dependence visible.
questions.hint: Ask what a test depends on, and whether it created that itself.

questions.topic: What A Coverage Figure Leaves Open
questions.learningObjective: explain the questions a coverage figure cannot answer
questions.stem: A suite reports full coverage of a module and the team is satisfied. Explain what the figure does not establish, and what has to be added by hand to cover the gap.

answer.exemplar: The figure records that each line was reached, and it records nothing about the values that reached it, so it cannot distinguish a line that behaves correctly for the inputs the suite happened to use from a line that is wrong for every input it has ever been given. It also cannot distinguish a line reached by a deliberate call from one reached by a mistake elsewhere in a test, because both look identical in the report. And it cannot see a line that does not exist yet, which is the more important half of the problem: a routine that has never handled a boundary, an empty collection, a value at the very edge of its range, or a second call that assumes the first succeeded has no lines to miss, so full coverage of what exists says nothing at all about what is missing. The gap is closed by hand and only by hand, and the questions worth asking are a fixed set. What happens with no input at all, and is that a deliberate answer or an accident. What happens one step past a boundary, in both directions rather than one. What happens the second time, since many defects are state that survived from the first call. What happens with a value of the wrong type that the caller promised would not arrive but a future caller might send anyway. What happens when a dependency fails, and whether the failure is reported or swallowed. Each of those is a case rather than a line, and writing them as cases is what turns a full figure into a suite somebody can trust. There is a second habit worth naming, which is to read the uncovered lines before celebrating the covered ones, because the line that has never run is usually the error path and the error path is usually the one nobody checked by hand. And a third is to treat a coverage figure that falls as a signal rather than as an accident, since a suite whose coverage drops when a new branch is added has just told you the new branch is untested.

questions.explanation: The figure records that lines were reached and nothing about the values that reached them, so a line that is wrong for every input the suite uses still counts as covered, and it cannot see a case that has no line yet, such as an empty input or a second call. Closing that gap means writing the cases by hand, and the fixed set worth asking about is the empty input, the boundary in both directions, the second call, a value of the wrong type, and a dependency that fails.

questions.topic: Why A Computed Value Beats A Stored One
questions.learningObjective: explain the failure a stored derived value allows
questions.stem: A class stores two values and also stores a third computed from them, and a change to one of the two leaves the third stale. Explain why computing on read removes that class of defect, and what it costs.

answer.exemplar: A stored derived value can only be correct at the moment it was written, so every later write to the values it was derived from opens a window in which it is wrong, and the code that has to close that window is the code that has to remember to recompute after every write. That is a rule about every future edit rather than a rule about the one place the value is defined, and rules of that kind are exactly the ones a later change forgets. Reading the third name through a computation removes the window entirely, because there is no moment at which a stored copy exists to be wrong, and the value is derived from the two current values every time anybody asks. The same argument is why a class that stores a total next to a list of prices is a class whose total has to be recomputed in every method that changes the list, and why the omission is so easy, since the compiler has no way to notice a method that changed a price and did not touch the total. The cost is real and worth stating plainly. Every read does the work again, so a value that is expensive to compute and read often should be computed once, and a class that genuinely needs that has to own the invalidation, which means a flag, a stored copy, and a method that knows when to refresh it. That machinery is the thing the computed form is avoiding, and it is worth paying for only when the computation is genuinely expensive or the reads are in a hot loop. There is also a debugging benefit that is easy to overlook. With a computed value, a wrong answer has one place it can be wrong, which is the computation, and a reader can check that one expression. With a stored value there are two places, the computation and every write that should have refreshed it, and a defect can be anywhere among them. The pattern is also what lets a value be validated on the way in, so an object cannot exist in an impossible state, and that is a stronger guarantee than keeping the invariant in each method separately.

questions.explanation: A stored derived value is correct only at the moment it was written, so every later write to what it came from opens a window in which it is wrong, and closing that window means a rule about every future edit that a later change will forget. Computing on read removes the window because no stored copy exists to be stale, and the cost is that the work is repeated on each read, which is worth paying for a value that is expensive to compute or read often, and then the class has to own invalidation itself.
questions.hint: Ask whether a stored copy can be wrong at a moment when nothing has just been written.

questions.topic: The Cost Of Pinning A Private Helper
questions.learningObjective: explain why a test of a private helper makes later change harder
questions.stem: A suite has a test that reaches straight into a helper marked private, and a colleague wants to simplify that helper. Explain what the test costs the colleague, and what the suite should assert instead.

answer.exemplar: The private mark is a promise to the next reader that this helper is free to change, and the test withdraws it. The colleague who simplifies the helper is not breaking the program, they are taking the change the mark advertised, and the test fails anyway, and now they face a choice between doing the work and either deleting a test that was added deliberately or finding a way to keep the old behaviour that the program no longer needs. Every one of those outcomes is worse for the codebase than the change they were trying to make, which is why a test of a private helper is a tax on every future edit rather than a contribution to confidence. The deeper problem is that the test is not about anything a user can observe. It states that a particular decomposition of the implementation is the one that will be used, and that is a claim about the code's shape rather than its behaviour, so it can be true while the program is broken and the program can be right while the test fails. What the suite should assert instead is the behaviour of the thing the private helper serves, because that is what a caller depends on and what a change has to preserve. Testing through the public face also covers the helper indirectly, including the case where the helper is wrong in a way that only shows up once the caller has used it, and it produces a failure message a reader can act on rather than one about a name they were told not to depend on. The legitimate exceptions are worth naming so the rule is not applied blindly. A helper that is genuinely intricate enough to have defects of its own is a sign it should be its own object with a public face, and its tests then become tests of that object rather than of somebody else's private corner. A helper that is pure, so it takes values and returns a value with no state of its own, is cheaper to pin than a stateful one, and the cost is lower though the argument still applies. A private name is not a barrier in the language, so nothing stops a test from reaching it, which is why this is a judgement a team makes deliberately rather than a rule the language enforces for it.

questions.explanation: The private mark promises the helper is free to change, and a test of it withdraws that promise, so the next person who simplifies the helper pays for a change that was always meant to be allowed, and the failure is about the code's shape rather than its behaviour. The suite should assert through the public face the helper serves, which covers the helper indirectly and produces a failure a reader can act on. questions.topic: Records Read By Their Header Names
questions.learningObjective: pair what a name-based reader hands back with the reason it is used
questions.stem:
A block with a header line is read by field name rather than by position, and two fields from two records are printed along with the record count. Which pair names what this program prints and why?

import csv, io
data = "name,age\namy,30\nbob,41\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)))
print(rows[0]["name"], rows[1]["age"], len(rows))

options.text: It prints amy, then 41, then two, because the header names the fields and is not itself a record
It prints amy, then 41, then three, because the header line is counted as a record
options.misconception: believes the header line is a record like the others

options.text: It prints amy, then 30, then two, because every record is read from the first row's fields
options.misconception: believes all records share the first record's values

options.text: It prints amy, then 41, then two, because the count includes the header as well
options.misconception: believes the count and the reader disagree about the header

questions.explanation: The header line supplies the names the fields are read by and is consumed as names rather than kept as a record, so there are two records, and the first record's name field and the second record's age field are read by the names the header declared. Reading by name rather than by position is the reason to use this reader, because a producer that reorders its columns then needs no change here. The answer counting the header is the belief to rule out first, because the reader has already used that line for its names and cannot also hand it back as data, and a program that wanted it would have to read the block a second time without the name-based reader.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader did with the header line, and what it counts as a record.
